data.content_ref: inline:The target is self-defeating on two levels. First, the mechanism's sole justification for preferring the most severe test is that it 'ensures' rapid error detection — an instrumental, outcome-valuing argument (the expected benefit of fast error elimination). This is precisely expected-utility reasoning: the agent selects the test whose outcome (quick learning) is most valuable. Yet the claim explicitly rejects expected utility as a rational metric. The target cannot coherently disown expected-utility reasoning while leaning on it as the only rationale for the very metric it proposes. Second, the mechanism's word 'ensuring' asserts a guarantee that errors will be found quickly, directly contradicting the claim's concession that acceptance 'costs us any guarantee of practical success or proximity to truth.' Rapid error detection is a practical success; guaranteeing it via 'ensuring' reintroduces exactly the guarantee the claim says is forfeited. The counterconditions do not cover this internal contradiction, because countercondition 3 only guards against justifying preference by minimizing practical-failure risk, not against the mechanism smuggling in an outcome-based guarantee and expected-utility reasoning to justify severity itself.
